facts.statement: Eight intermediate (issuing) CAs in our Global TLS business were revoked because their published keys were weak.
Intermediate keys were revoked, not root keys. The weakness was in the keys of the eight intermediates.
the affected intermediates had not issued publicly trusted end-entity certificates
The roughly 30,800 certificates issued under the affected G3 hierarchies belong to a client ecosystem in the United States.
blocking the affected certificates in Firefox using OneCRL
We are already in the process of moving our impacted G3 customers and our broader non-impacted TLS customers to alternate certificates at no cost.
there has been no compromise of our infrastructure or customer data.

editorial.title: eMudhra weak intermediate keys prompt browser distrust and certificate migration
editorial.summary: eMudhra says eight intermediate certificate authorities had weak, recoverable keys and were revoked. Mozilla blocked the affected certificates in Firefox. The issuer says its root key was not compromised, while root-store distrust and certificate migration create a separate operational impact for customers.
editorial.why_it_matters: Certificate trust depends on both the issuing hierarchy and client update behavior. A revocation can protect some clients promptly while stale trust stores and services that do not check revocation need separate review.
editorial.action: Identify certificates and trust stores that chain to the affected eMudhra hierarchy; follow the issuer and platform vendors’ replacement guidance. Update client trust stores where applicable and verify service continuity after reissuing certificates. Preserve any evidence of suspicious certificate use for investigation.

sections.heading: What the issuer and browser report
paragraphs: eMudhra says eight Global TLS intermediate authorities were created with weak published keys and then revoked. Its statement expressly distinguishes the intermediate keys from the root key: the root was distrusted as a precaution, not reported as cryptographically compromised. Mozilla says it blocked the affected intermediates in Firefox through OneCRL.

The issuer also says the weak intermediates had not issued publicly trusted end-entity certificates, based on its investigation to date. That statement limits a direct claim about certificates signed by those intermediates. It does not eliminate the separate migration work caused by distrust of a higher-level hierarchy.

sections.heading: Separate the two certificate scopes
paragraphs: eMudhra reports roughly 30,800 certificates under affected G3 hierarchies in one United States client ecosystem. Those certificates are not the same as certificates issued by the eight weak intermediates. Operators should trace their actual chain and trust-store behavior instead of treating every eMudhra certificate as having a weak private key.

Browser blocking, certificate revocation and root-store changes can take effect at different times across clients. The practical check is whether each client and service accepts the intended replacement chain. Use the current issuer and browser-program notices to determine the right transition path.

sections.heading: What remains unproven
paragraphs: The issuer says it found no infrastructure or customer-data compromise. That is its current investigation statement, not proof that no attempted misuse occurred anywhere. This report makes no claim that the root private key was stolen or that forged certificates were observed.

For incident response, preserve certificate chains, client errors and trust-store versions if unexpected behavior appears. For routine remediation, prioritize the services and clients actually using the affected hierarchy and confirm successful replacement.
